classification.difficultyReason: Factor the curve difference to find three intersections, identify the upper curve on each interval, and integrate the two regions; symmetry is an optional shortcut.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the points of intersection of $y=x^{2}(1-x)$ and $y=x(1-x)^{2}$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}x^{2}(1-x)&=x(1-x)^{2}\\x^{2}(1-x)-x(1-x)^{2}&=0\\x(1-x)[x-(1-x)]&=0\\x(1-x)(2x-1)&=0\\x&=0,\;1,\;\frac12\end{aligned}$$
For $x=0$, $y=0$, giving $(0,0)$.

For $x=\frac12$,
$$y=\left(\frac12\right)^{2}\left(1-\frac12\right)=\frac18,$$
giving $\left(\frac12,\frac18\right)$.

For $x=1$, $y=0$, giving $(1,0)$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the area bounded by the two curves.

answer.worked:
Let $f(x)=x^{2}(1-x)$ and $g(x)=x(1-x)^{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)-g(x)&=x(1-x)[x-(1-x)]\\f(x)-g(x)&=x(1-x)(2x-1).\end{aligned}$$
For $0<x<\frac12$, $f(x)<g(x)$, so the second curve is above the first.

For $\frac12<x<1$, $f(x)>g(x)$, so the first curve is above the second.

Reflection in $x=\frac12$ interchanges the curves, so the two regions have equal area.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_{0}^{1/2}\left[x(1-x)^{2}-x^{2}(1-x)\right]\,dx\\A&=2\int_{0}^{1/2}x(1-x)(1-2x)\,dx\\A&=2\int_{0}^{1/2}(x-3x^{2}+2x^{3})\,dx\\A&=2\left[\frac{x^{2}}2-x^{3}+\frac{x^{4}}2\right]_{0}^{1/2}\\A&=2\left(\frac18-\frac18+\frac1{32}\right)\\A&=\frac1{16}\text{ units}^{2}.\end{aligned}$$
